examples.answer: A detector that always says normal can look accurate while finding none of the rare frauds. I would inspect the precision recall tradeoff and price the cost of blocking a real customer against the cost of letting fraud through. The holdout should keep the same fraud frequency as traffic. We can upweight or oversample fraud while fitting, but not in the holdout. I would calibrate scores on a separate sample with the real traffic mix.
Accuracy by itself can reward a model for ignoring the rare class. We can weight the rare class more heavily in the training loss. I would also change the dashboard font.

Accuracy alone is sufficient for rare disease screening. Balance the validation and test sets to half positive before reporting production precision. Calibrate the scores on that balanced test set too.

first subtract each feature mean then rotate into perpendicular axes ordered by the spread they explain keeping the leading axes gives the least squared reconstruction error among linear projections I would standardize mixed units first or the largest units can decide the directions the axes with the most spread need not separate the labels and a straight linear subspace cannot follow a curved manifold
PCA finds orthogonal directions with high variance after centering. A dollar-valued feature can dominate a millimeter-valued one, so I would consider standardization.

PCA chooses the directions with the smallest variance and guarantees the best class separation. Standardizing the inputs cannot change the components. A linear PCA projection can represent any curved manifold exactly.

Completely random missingness is unrelated to anything measured or unmeasured. Missing at random can depend on recorded fields; not at random can depend on the absent value itself. Throwing away incomplete rows can therefore select a biased population. I would learn the replacement values from training rows only and consider a flag saying that an entry was absent.
If the chance of a missing income depends on the income we cannot observe, that is MNAR. I would fit an imputer on training data only and try a missing-value flag.

MCAR means missingness depends on observed age. MAR means it depends on the missing salary itself. MNAR means it is independent of everything. Dropping incomplete rows never changes the population. Learn replacement values on the full dataset before splitting.

batch norm estimates a mean and spread for each channel across the minibatch layer norm instead computes them across the features of a single example or token at evaluation batch norm uses running estimates saved during fitting layer norm needs no other examples so it works with small batches and changing sequence lengths in transformers
Layer norm uses statistics within one token rather than across examples. That makes it independent of the batch size, which is useful for transformer sequences.

Batch norm normalizes the features inside each token. Layer norm estimates statistics across the minibatch. At inference batch norm must recompute statistics from the current batch and layer norm cannot run with one example.

I would run suitable operations in a narrower format and retain higher precision for numerically sensitive parts. Half precision can lose tiny derivatives to zero and saturate large activations. Multiplying the loss before backprop and unscaling afterwards can rescue those tiny FP16 gradients. BF16 has more exponent bits than FP16 so its range is wider. I would compare loss, gradient health and quality rather than assuming the format change is harmless.
FP16 can overflow a large activation or underflow a tiny gradient. BF16 has a wider exponent range. I would check numerical errors and held-out quality after switching formats.

FP16 has a wider exponent range than BF16 and never underflows. Loss scaling protects small gradients by making the loss smaller. Every operation should use low precision because it preserves all results exactly.

Self attention forms Q K and V from the same stream. In the encoder decoder link, the decoder provides the query and the encoded source provides keys and values. A triangular target mask rules out looking at later target positions. This lets us fit autoregressive predictions in parallel without revealing the answer tokens that come later.
The cross-attention queries come from the decoder, while its keys and values come from the encoder. Self-attention gets all three from the same sequence.

Self-attention takes its queries from the encoder and its keys from the decoder. Cross-attention takes all three from one sequence. A causal mask reveals future target words so the network can copy the targets during autoregressive training.

Every token is compared with every other token in dense attention, so doubling length roughly quadruples the score work. Keeping the whole score grid also takes quadratic space. FlashAttention changes the IO schedule and avoids writing that grid out, but exact dense attention still does quadratic arithmetic. Restricting connections to a sparse or local pattern reduces work by changing the operation. During decoding I would retain earlier keys and values so we do not project the whole prefix again.
Keeping an all-pairs attention matrix costs quadratic memory. Caching past keys and values avoids computing them again for every new token.

Ordinary dense attention has linear sequence cost and a linear-sized score matrix. FlashAttention makes exact dense attention linear arithmetic without changing the connections. KV caching deliberately recomputes all old keys and values at each step.

I want a shared definition for a feature so fitting and live prediction use the same meaning. Historical examples must be joined only to values that existed at their event times, never later updates. The offline store serves training scans while the online store handles fast point lookups. Fresh values and identical transformations help keep training and serving inputs aligned.
Point-in-time retrieval should use only values known at the example timestamp. The offline side supports large training jobs and the online side provides low-latency lookups.

Training and serving should implement feature definitions independently. A point-in-time join should always choose the newest value even if it arrived after the label. Feature freshness and transform consistency cannot affect prediction quality.

For exact frequencies I need a counter for every distinct key, so memory grows with cardinality. After counting, I can retain the largest k counts with a min heap of size k. If the counters do not fit, a sketch or a heavy-hitter summary gives a fixed-memory approximation. I would state its error guarantee and ask whether another pass is available to verify candidate frequencies.
An exact frequency table needs space proportional to the distinct keys. A count-min sketch is an option when fixed memory matters more than exact counts.
A k-element heap alone counts every distinct item exactly in constant memory for any stream. Approximate sketches never make errors and never require any assumptions or another pass.

under the null hypothesis the p value is the probability of data at least this extreme it does not tell me the probability that the null is true a tiny p value can go with an effect too small to matter to the business repeatedly checking until the result becomes significant or trying many tests raises the chance of a false discovery
A p-value is not the probability that the null is true. Statistical significance alone does not tell us the size of the benefit or whether it matters to the product.

A p-value of 0.02 proves the null has a two percent chance of being true. A small p-value guarantees a large business effect. Repeating the test and stopping whenever it becomes significant cannot raise the false-positive rate.

I would inspect the document structures and the questions people actually ask first. Cutting at a fixed token count is easy but may bisect an idea; splitting at headings, paragraphs or code boundaries respects the content structure. Tiny pieces can be specific matches but lack the surrounding explanation, while large pieces keep that explanation at the cost of less focused embeddings and extra prompt tokens. Overlap between neighboring windows keeps a boundary-crossing idea available. I would choose the settings using retrieval measurements on labeled queries.

First inspect actual documents and the patterns in user questions. Overlapping neighboring windows preserves ideas at split boundaries. Pick the settings by measuring retrieval quality on labeled queries.

Document structure and user questions are irrelevant. A fixed token split always preserves entire ideas. Bigger chunks always improve specificity and reduce prompt cost. Never overlap neighboring windows, and choose the settings without any evaluation data.

Write down the criteria, the score scale and example responses for each level. Reverse the answer ordering to check position effects and avoid rewarding extra length just for being long. Use a judge from a different family to reduce favoritism toward its own model. Compare with human-rated examples initially and keep measuring that agreement as things change.
I would define the criteria and a scoring scale with examples of each score. To reduce self-preference I would select a judge from another model family.

Do not specify any criteria or examples. Always put our preferred answer first and reward longer responses automatically. Use the same model family as both contestant and judge to maximize self-preference. Human agreement is irrelevant and never needs to be measured.
